title: Power BI in Microsoft Fabric: A Practitioner's Complete Reference
summary: A comprehensive reference covering Power BI's role as the analytics and visualization workload of Microsoft Fabric — from core concepts and content types through workspace collaboration, security, Direct Lake internals, query performance mechanics, and practical best practices for production deployments.
body_md:
Power BI is Microsoft's business analytics platform for turning data into insights, and within Microsoft Fabric it operates as the dedicated analytics and visualization workload [S1]. That single sentence carries more weight than it first appears: Power BI is not an external tool bolted onto Fabric — it is one of Fabric's core workloads, sharing the same capacity, the same storage layer (OneLake), and the same governance infrastructure as every other Fabric experience [S1].

For practitioners who already use Power BI, the transition to Fabric is deliberately frictionless. Existing Power BI content and workspaces carry over without migration, users sign in with their existing Power BI or Microsoft 365 accounts, and the Power BI interface remains familiar while Fabric layers on additional capabilities [S1]. The incremental nature of that layering is intentional: your dashboards keep working while you adopt OneLake integration, Direct Lake mode, and Fabric's notebook-based data engineering at whatever pace your organization requires.

This article is a full reference covering every verified fact in the knowledge base — components, content types, collaboration model, security, Direct Lake mechanics, query internals, and the patterns and antipatterns that matter in production. Where the knowledge base has gaps (L4/L5 internals for general Power BI capacity behavior, for example), those gaps are called out explicitly rather than papered over.

---

## Components and Deployment Modes

Power BI's main components are Power BI Desktop, the cloud-based Power BI service, and mobile apps [S1]:

- **Power BI Desktop** is a Windows authoring application for data modeling and report design. It connects to more than 100 data source types, transforms data through Power Query Editor, builds semantic models with DAX (measures, calculated columns, relationships), offers more than 30 built-in and custom visuals, and includes advanced tooling such as the Performance Analyzer, external tools support, and composite models [S1].
- **The Power BI service** is the cloud layer for publishing, sharing, and collaboration. It adds workspaces, apps, dataflows, shared semantic models across reports, scheduled refresh, email subscriptions, alerts, Q&A natural-language queries, embedding, and data export on top of authored content [S1][S2].
- **Mobile apps** deliver on-the-go viewing of reports and dashboards on phones and tablets [S1].

For organizations that must keep reporting on-premises, Power BI Report Server provides a hybrid path that retains the option to move to the cloud later, avoiding the need to build a parallel reporting stack [S1].

The recommended division of labor is to author and model in Power BI Desktop, publish to the Power BI service for team sharing and collaboration, and use the mobile apps for consumption on the move [S1].

---

## Content Types: Reports, Dashboards, and Apps

Understanding the three primary content types is prerequisite to a coherent workspace design.

### Reports

A Power BI report is one or more pages of interactive visuals, text, and graphics that draw from exactly one semantic model [S2]. Reports are typically organized around a specific set of questions — for example, sales performance by region, or inventory aging by product category. The constraint of one semantic model per report is not a limitation to work around; it is a design boundary that makes source-of-truth governance tractable.

### Dashboards

A Power BI dashboard is a single screen composed of tiles — interactive visuals, text, and graphics — used to monitor key metrics at a glance [S2]. Unlike a report, a dashboard is always one screen, and its tiles can be sourced from multiple reports and multiple semantic models [S2]. Dashboards are a consumption surface for executives and operators who need a single view across domains, not an authoring surface for analysts who need drill-down depth.

### Apps

A Power BI app bundles dashboards, reports, and semantic models into a single package for distribution to individuals, groups, or an entire organization [S2]. Publishing an app is the preferred way for designers to distribute related dashboards and reports to a large audience, rather than sharing items one at a time [S2]. The app model separates the workspace (where content is authored and managed) from the audience view (what consumers see), which protects in-progress work from leaking to downstream consumers.

### Paginated Reports

Pageinated reports, built with Power BI Report Builder, target structured pixel-perfect printable output such as invoices [S1]. They complement — rather than replace — interactive reports: use paginated reports when the output is a document that must render identically on every page at any zoom level, and use interactive reports for exploration and drill-down.

---

## Workspaces and Roles

Activity in the Power BI service divides into two roles: designers and creators who build, organize, and publish content, and consumers and business users who view, filter, and drill into that content to make decisions [S2].

Workspaces are the collaborative containers where designers manage collections of dashboards, reports, and other items [S2]. Access is controlled through four workspace roles:

- **Admin** — full control including role management
- **Member** — can publish and manage all content
- **Contributor** — can add and edit content
- **Viewer** — read-only access

In Fabric, the same workspace that holds Power BI content can also hold lakehouses, notebooks, pipelines, warehouses, and other Fabric item types [S2]. This co-location is architecturally significant: a data engineer writing to a lakehouse and a report developer building a semantic model can work in the same workspace, simplifying handoffs and reducing the friction of cross-item references.

---

## Power BI in Microsoft Fabric: Shared vs. Power BI-Specific Features

Within Fabric, Power BI gains access to platform-level features shared with all other workloads, while retaining a set of capabilities that are Power BI-specific [S1].

Choosing how a semantic model connects to that data — Import, DirectQuery, or Direct Lake — is one of the most consequential architecture decisions in a Fabric deployment, so the diagram below walks through that decision as a branching tree.

![Decision tree for choosing a Power BI semantic model storage mode: Import, DirectQuery, or Direct Lake, including the Direct Lake on OneLake vs on SQL sub-decision, fallback triggers, tradeoffs, and guardrails](/diagrams/power-bi-storage-mode-decision.svg)

**Platform-level features (shared with all Fabric workloads):**
- OneLake integration and Direct Lake mode
- Dataflows Gen2 and notebooks
- Purview-based security and governance
- Data Activator alerting
- Copilot AI assistance

**Power BI-specific capabilities:**
- Power BI Desktop authoring application
- The Power BI service (publishing, collaboration, scheduled refresh)
- Paginated reports and Report Builder
- The visuals marketplace
- Q&A natural-language query
- Goals and scorecards

This distinction matters for licensing and architecture planning: platform features require Fabric capacity, while Power BI-specific features are covered by Power BI licensing (Pro, Premium Per User, or Premium capacity).

---

## Data Sources: Dataflows, Excel, and Semantic Models

Reports in the Power BI service are built over semantic models. Those models can be fed data in several ways.

Dataflows in the Power BI service store reusable, centralized data-preparation steps — but they are now designated legacy [S2]. Fabric's Dataflows Gen2 is the platform-level successor and the recommended path for new work [S2].

Excel workbooks uploaded to the Power BI service can be viewed directly or used as data sources feeding reports and dashboards [S2]. This is a common entry point for teams that already maintain analytical workbooks and want to surface them alongside purpose-built reports.

Reports against a semantic model can be created from many entry points: Power BI Desktop via the OneLake catalog, the workspace context menu, the model details page, or web modeling's create-new-report option [S3]. The breadth of entry points reflects Fabric's intent to make the semantic model the reusable analytical hub, not a side artifact of report authoring.

---

## Copilot in Power BI

Copilot in Power BI is an AI assistant for building reports, analyzing data, and generating natural-language summaries [S2]. It is enabled by default, but only functions on a paid Fabric capacity of F2 or higher, or Power BI Premium P1 or higher [S2]. Teams planning to use Copilot should verify their capacity SKU before including it in user-facing workflows.

---

## Direct Lake: The Architecture That Connects Power BI to OneLake

Direct Lake is the feature that makes Power BI a native Fabric citizen rather than an integration. It is a semantic-model storage mode in which the model reads Delta tables straight from OneLake, avoiding both data import and DirectQuery, and pairs import-like performance with DirectQuery-like freshness [S5].

![Power BI consumption over semantic models](/content/diagrams/power-bi-consumption.svg)

Before Direct Lake, Power BI offered two storage modes: **import**, where data is copied into the model's in-memory VertiPaq engine (fast but stale until refreshed), and **DirectQuery**, where every visual fires a live SQL query against the source (always fresh but often slow). Direct Lake mode in the Analysis Services engine lets Power BI semantic models read Delta Parquet data straight from OneLake, delivering import-mode speed without maintaining a copied dataset [S6].

When a report visual requests data from a Direct Lake table, the semantic model reads the Delta table in OneLake directly and may retain recently accessed data in an in-memory cache to serve subsequent queries efficiently [S3].

Direct Lake mode lets reports query data sitting in OneLake directly, without importing it into the model or maintaining a separate cache [S1].

### Two Flavors of Direct Lake

Direct Lake comes in two storage-mode flavors [S7]:

- **Direct Lake on OneLake** — uses OneLake security, offers richer modeling features, and delivers faster query performance.
- **Direct Lake on SQL** — needed when SQL analytics endpoint security rules apply under delegated identity, or when DirectQuery fallback is required.

Direct Lake on OneLake is chosen for OneLake security, more modeling features, and faster query performance [S8]. Direct Lake on SQL applies when SQL analytics endpoint security rules are needed or DirectQuery fallback is required [S8].

Power BI Desktop and the Power BI service create only Direct Lake on OneLake models [S7]. The SQL analytics endpoint page is the creation path that offers a choice between both flavors [S7]. When creating a model from the SQL analytics endpoint, the type dialog defaults to Direct Lake on OneLake if the endpoint runs in user identity mode, and to Direct Lake on SQL if it runs in delegated identity mode [S7].

### Identifying the Flavor

You can identify a model's Direct Lake flavor from its M expression in TMDL view: Direct Lake on OneLake uses the Azure Data Lake Storage connector, while Direct Lake on SQL uses the SQL Server or OneLake.SqlAnalytics connector [S7].

Over XMLA, a Direct Lake model is recognizable by a database `compatibilityLevel` of 1604 or higher, partitions whose mode is `directLake`, and partitions that reference a shared expression as their data source [S7].

### Tooling

Direct Lake models can be developed beyond the browser with XMLA-compliant tools such as SSMS 19.1+, community tools, or programmatically from Fabric notebooks via semantic link and semantic-link-labs [S7].

---

## Security

### Power BI Service Security

The Power BI service implements security and oversight through row-level security (RLS), sensitivity labels, usage metrics, and audit logs [S1].

### Direct Lake and Network Isolation

Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active [S4 (private-links source)]. Semantic models relying on Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints, making this connection mode incompatible with the most restrictive Fabric network isolation posture [S4 (private-links source)]. Teams evaluating tenant-level private links must account for this constraint before committing to that network posture.

---

## How Direct Lake Works: Framing, Transcoding, and Memory Residency

This section covers the L3 and L4/L5 internals that determine why Direct Lake behaves the way it does in production.

### Lazy Column Loading

Direct Lake loads column data from OneLake lazily: nothing is read until a query first touches a column, and the load set includes not just columns the query names but also those needed by relationships and measures [S9]. The consequence is that the first query to touch a cold column pays a transcoding cost; subsequent queries that hit the same column find it already resident.

### Framing

Framing is a metadata-only refresh that typically finishes in seconds: the model reads the latest Delta table version and rebinds itself to the current Parquet file set, establishing the new baseline for future transcoding [S9].

An automatic-updates model setting, on by default, reframes Direct Lake tables whenever the underlying OneLake data changes [S9]. Turn it off to control data visibility through manual or scheduled framing — useful when Delta data is transient (for example, mid-ETL): disabling automatic updates and framing deliberately yields consistent results during long-running loads [S9].

Direct Lake queries reflect the Delta table state as of the most recent successful framing operation, not the live table, so writes landing after the last frame remain invisible until the next one [S9].

During incremental framing, Direct Lake reads each table's Delta log and evicts only the column segments tied to removed row groups, while dictionaries are kept and merely extended with new values to avoid re-transcoding [S10].

### Memory Residency States

A Direct Lake model occupies one of four memory-residency states — cold, semiwarm, warm, or hot — with query latency improving at each step [S10]. Hot adds populated VertiScan caches on top of fully resident column data [S10].

A resident column can be evicted for three reasons: a refresh (framing) after the source Delta table changed, prolonged non-use by queries, or general memory pressure on the capacity from concurrent operations [S9].

### Transcoding: From Parquet to VertiPaq

On a cold-state query, Direct Lake must merge the per-row-group local Parquet dictionaries of each needed column into a single global VertiPaq dictionary; a Delta table with more row groups takes longer to transcode [S10].

Transcoding is usually a direct remap of Parquet data IDs to VertiPaq IDs when both sides use RLE/Bit-Packing hybrid encoding. If a Parquet file used plain or delta encoding instead, Direct Lake must re-encode the values, which slows column loading [S10].

V-Order speeds Direct Lake twice over: it raises RLE compression quality so columns stream into memory faster during transcoding, and it lets VertiScan compute results directly on compressed data without a decompression step [S10].

The total row-group count across a Delta table's Parquet files maps one-to-one to the number of VertiPaq segments per model column, so many tiny row groups produce many tiny column segments and degrade query performance [S10].

For large tables, Direct Lake prefers column segments of roughly 1 to 16 million rows; Fabric may write even larger row groups for compressible data, which is tolerable, but row groups well under 1 million rows hurt performance [S10].

### Cold Multi-Table DAX Queries

Answering a cold multi-table DAX query also requires Direct Lake to build join indexes from the relationship key columns (loading their dictionaries plus the one-side key segments) and to load any Delta deletion vectors so deleted rows are excluded [S10].

### DirectQuery Fallback (Direct Lake on SQL only)

DirectQuery fallback exists only in Direct Lake on SQL; documented triggers are querying a SQL-endpoint view, querying a table with SQL-endpoint row-level security, and a Delta table exceeding capacity guardrails [S9].

A fallen-back query reads the SQL analytics endpoint directly and therefore returns the latest data, escaping the framing point-in-time — at the cost of typically slower performance [S9].

Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back to DirectQuery and skips SQL-endpoint coupling entirely, which enables more efficient DAX query plans since no SQL security check is needed [S9].

Fallback behavior for Direct Lake on SQL models is governed by the model's `DirectLakeBehavior` property; the property has no effect on Direct Lake on OneLake models [S9].

In Direct Lake on SQL, the shared expression points at the SQL analytics endpoint, which is consulted only for schema and security discovery — actual data is still read straight from OneLake unless the query falls back to DirectQuery [S7].

In Direct Lake on OneLake, the shared expression points straight at the OneLake storage location, and OneLake APIs handle schema discovery, security checks, and data loading with no SQL endpoint involved [S7].

### Capacity Guardrails

Framing can fail when a Delta table breaches capacity guardrails, such as exceeding 10,000 Parquet files in a single table [S9].

Direct Lake does not use Delta or Parquet statistics for row-group or file skipping when loading column data, so pruning optimizations that help other query engines do not reduce its transcoding work [S10].

## Best Practices

The following recommendations come directly from verified pattern-type claims in the knowledge base.

**Authoring workflow.** Author and model in Power BI Desktop, publish to the Power BI service for team sharing, and use mobile apps for on-the-go consumption [S1]. This division of labor keeps Desktop as the single source-of-truth for model definitions.

**App-based distribution.** Publish apps when distributing related dashboards and reports to a large audience, rather than sharing items one at a time [S2]. Apps decouple the authoring workspace from the consumer view, protecting work-in-progress from leaking downstream.

**On-premises hybrid.** Organizations that must keep reporting on-premises should use Power BI Report Server and retain the option to migrate to the cloud later, rather than building a parallel reporting stack [S1].

**Controlled framing during ETL.** Disable automatic updates and frame deliberately when Delta data is transient (mid-ETL), to prevent queries from seeing partial or inconsistent data [S9].

**Identify the Direct Lake flavor from TMDL.** Use the M expression connector type in TMDL view to confirm whether a model is Direct Lake on OneLake or Direct Lake on SQL before applying security or fallback configuration [S7].

**Delta table partitioning for Direct Lake.** Partition Delta tables only on low-cardinality columns; Microsoft suggests staying under approximately 100–200 distinct values [S10]. Over-partitioning multiplies small Parquet files and row groups, inflating segment counts in the model and degrading query performance.

**File sizing for Direct Lake.** A 1 GB BinSize target is recommended when writing Delta tables that back Power BI Direct Lake semantic models, because larger files align with the Direct Lake loading pattern and reduce the number of segment loads needed [S11].

---

## What Goes Wrong: Antipatterns to Avoid

The following antipatterns are drawn from verified claims tagged as `antipattern` in the knowledge base.

### Basing Direct Lake on SQL Tables on SQL Views

Basing a Direct Lake on SQL model table on a SQL view forces every query against that table into DirectQuery fallback, which usually slows it down [S7]. Prefer base tables for Direct Lake on SQL models. Reserve SQL views for scenarios where the fallback to DirectQuery is intentional and the performance tradeoff is acceptable.

### Using Delta Overwrite Mode Behind Direct Lake

Loading a Delta table with the Overwrite option wipes the table's commit history, defeating incremental framing and forcing a full cold-state reload of all segments, dictionaries, and join indexes on the next query [S10]. Use append or merge-based load patterns instead, so that incremental framing can identify only the changed row groups and avoid re-transcoding unchanged data.

### Vacuuming Too Aggressively

A framed Direct Lake model is pinned to a specific Delta commit version; vacuuming must not remove the Parquet files of that version before the next reframe, or user queries fail when the referenced files are gone [S10]. Set vacuum retention windows that are comfortably longer than the typical interval between framing operations.

### Enabling Block Public Internet Access with Direct Lake

Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active [S4]. Semantic models using Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints. If your security posture requires blocking all public internet access at the tenant level, Direct Lake mode cannot be used — this is an architectural constraint, not a configuration to tune around.

---

## Worked Example: Retail Sales Reporting Over a Fabric Lakehouse

This scenario shows how the verified mechanics fit together end-to-end.

**Setup.** A retail organization runs daily ETL that writes sales transaction data into a Delta table in a Fabric lakehouse. The table is partitioned by `sales_region` (fewer than 50 distinct values) and written using Optimized Write with a 1 GB BinSize target [S11]. V-Order is enabled at write time [S10].

**Semantic model creation.** A report developer opens Power BI Desktop, connects to the OneLake catalog, and creates a Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model over the sales Delta table and a separate products dimension table [S3][S7]. No data is imported; the model holds only schema metadata and DAX measure definitions.

**Framing control.** Because ETL runs from 02:00 to 04:00 and partially overwrites staging data mid-run, the developer disables automatic updates on the semantic model and configures a scheduled frame at 05:00 — after ETL completes [S9]. This prevents business users from querying a mid-ETL state. *Inference:* the 05:00 frame time was chosen based on ETL completion; the correct window for a given organization depends on its pipeline SLA.

**First query of the day.** When the first report page loads at 08:00, the model is cold. Direct Lake reads the `sales_amount`, `sales_region`, `product_id` columns and the join key columns from the Delta Parquet files [S9]. Because V-Order is enabled, transcoding is a fast RLE remap rather than a re-encode pass [S10]. The column segments are loaded into VertiPaq memory and the model enters warm state. Subsequent queries hit resident data.

**Memory pressure.** At peak reporting time (09:00–10:00), concurrent capacity usage causes some column segments from an infrequently queried table to be evicted [S9]. When a user loads a report page touching those columns, Direct Lake reloads them transparently — the user sees a slightly slower first response, then warm-state speed.

**Distribution.** The developer publishes the report to a Fabric workspace and creates a Power BI app packaging the report and a summary dashboard [S2]. The app is distributed to the regional sales team. Regional managers consume dashboards on mobile; analysts drill into the report pages on desktop.

**Security.** Row-level security is defined on the semantic model to restrict each sales manager to their own region [S1]. Because the model is Direct Lake on OneLake (not Direct Lake on SQL), no SQL endpoint security rules are needed and no DirectQuery fallback is triggered [S9].
